Video Tag

Definition
The <video> tag is used to embed video content in an HTML document. It supports various attributes to control playback, appearance, and behavior. Videos can be in formats like MP4, WebM, or OGV.
src
Specifies the source URL of the video file. It can be a local path or an online link. Multiple <source> tags can be used for different formats.
height & width
Control the dimensions of the video player in pixels or percentages.
controls
Adds playback controls like play, pause, volume, and progress bar to the video player.
autoplay
Automatically starts playing the video when the page loads. Note: Many browsers block autoplay without user interaction.
muted
Starts the video with sound muted. Useful with autoplay to avoid browser restrictions.
loop
Restarts the video automatically after it finishes playing.
poster
Displays a placeholder image while the video is loading or before playback starts.
preload
Specifies how the video should be loaded: "none" (no preload), "metadata" (load metadata only), "auto" (load entire video).

Example

Embedding Websites

Definition
Embedding allows you to include external content like videos, maps, or other websites directly into your HTML page using the <iframe> tag. This creates an inline frame within your document.
src
Specifies the URL of the content to embed, such as a YouTube video or Google Maps.
width & height
Define the dimensions of the embedded content in pixels.
frameborder
Controls whether a border is displayed around the iframe. Value "0" removes the border.
allow
Specifies permissions for the embedded content, such as "accelerometer", "autoplay", "fullscreen", etc.
allowfullscreen
Allows the embedded content to be displayed in fullscreen mode when supported.
title
Provides a title for the iframe, improving accessibility for screen readers.
loading
Controls when the iframe content loads: "lazy" (load when needed) or "eager" (load immediately).

Examples

YouTube Video

Google Maps

Audio Tag

Definition
The <audio> tag is used to embed audio content in an HTML document. It supports various attributes to control playback and appearance. Audio files can be in formats like MP3, WAV, or OGG.
src
Specifies the source URL of the audio file. It can be a local path or an online link. Multiple <source> tags can be used for different formats.
controls
Adds playback controls like play, pause, and volume to the audio player.
autoplay
Automatically starts playing the audio when the page loads. Note: Many browsers block autoplay.
muted
Starts the audio with sound muted.
loop
Restarts the audio automatically after it finishes.
preload
Specifies how the audio should be loaded: "none", "metadata", or "auto".
volume
Sets the initial volume level (0.0 to 1.0), though it's not widely supported.

Example

Elements

Definition
HTML elements are the building blocks of web pages. They consist of an opening tag, content, and a closing tag. Elements can be block-level or inline.

Block Elements

Definition
Block elements always start on a new line and take up the full width available. They create a "block" of content.
Examples
<h1>-<h6> (headings), <div> (division), <p> (paragraph), <ol> (ordered list), <ul> (unordered list), <table> (table), etc.
Characteristics
They stack vertically, can contain other block or inline elements, and have default margins/padding.

Inline Elements

Definition
Inline elements do not start on a new line and only take up as much width as necessary. They flow within the text.
Examples
<span> (generic inline container), <a> (anchor/link), <strong> (strong emphasis), <em> (emphasis), <img> (image), <br> (line break), etc.
Characteristics
They appear in the flow of text, cannot contain block elements, and respect text formatting.

Attributes

Definition
Attributes provide additional information about HTML elements. They are always placed inside the opening tag and usually come in key-value pairs, e.g., height="100px". Attributes modify the behavior or appearance of elements.
Purpose
Used to give properties to tags/elements, control functionality, styling, and accessibility.

Types of Attributes

Core/Global Attributes

Attributes that can be used in any HTML element.

id
Provides a unique identifier for an element, used for styling, scripting, and linking.
class
Assigns one or more class names to an element for styling and grouping.
style
Applies inline CSS styles directly to an element.
title
Provides additional information displayed as a tooltip on hover.
height & width
Specify the dimensions of the element (for applicable elements like images, videos).
hidden
A boolean attribute that hides the element from view.
lang
Specifies the language of the element's content for accessibility and styling.
tabindex
Controls the tab order for keyboard navigation.
contenteditable
Makes the element's content editable by the user.

Element-Specific Attributes

Attributes that are used only with specific elements.

href
Used with <a> tags to specify the destination URL of a link.
src
Used with media elements like <img>, <video>, <audio> to specify the source path.
alt
Provides alternative text for <img> elements if the image fails to load.
type
In <input> tags, specifies the input type (e.g., text, password, email).
value
Sets the default value in form inputs or the value of buttons.
target
Used with <a> tags to specify where to open the linked document.
placeholder
Provides hint text in input fields that disappears when typing.
required
Makes a form field mandatory for submission.

Anchor Tag

Definition
The <a> tag, or anchor tag, is used to create hyperlinks in web pages. It allows navigation between pages or sections.
href
Specifies the destination URL of the link. Can be absolute (external site) or relative (within the same site).
target
Specifies where to open the linked document. Values: "_blank" (new tab), "_self" (same tab), "_parent", "_top".
title
Provides additional information about the link, displayed as a tooltip on hover.
rel
Specifies the relationship between the current document and the linked document. Values like "noopener", "noreferrer" for security.
download
Causes the browser to download the linked resource instead of navigating to it.

HTML Basics

History of HTML

HTML stands for HyperText Markup Language. It was created by Tim Berners-Lee in 1991 to structure content on the web. HTML is the standard language used to build web pages and applications.

Created by / Used for

Created by
Tim Berners-Lee at CERN.
Used for
Structuring web content using tags to define headings, paragraphs, links, images, lists, tables, and forms.

HTML Versions

  • HTML 1.0 - First version published in 1991.
  • HTML 2.0 - Standardized version in 1995.
  • HTML 3.2 / 4.0 - Added more tags and layout features.
  • HTML5 - Current major version, introduced modern semantic tags and multimedia support.

Main Tags

The main HTML tags create the page structure and content. Basic tags include:

  • <html> - Root element of an HTML document.
  • <head> - Contains metadata, title, and links to styles/scripts.
  • <title> - Sets the browser tab title.
  • <meta> - Provides page metadata like charset and viewport.
  • <body> - Contains the visible page content.
  • <h1>–<h6> - Heading tags.
  • <p> - Paragraph text.
  • <a> - Hyperlink anchor tag.
  • <img> - Embeds images.
  • <ul>, <ol>, <li> - List tags.
  • <table>, <tr>, <th>, <td> - Table tags.
  • <form>, <input>, <label>, <textarea>, <select> - Form tags.
  • <div> - Block-level container.
  • <span> - Inline container.
  • <header>, <nav>, <div>, <article>, <footer>, <aside> - Semantic diving tags.

Basic HTML Tag Definitions

<html>
The root element of an HTML page.
<head>
Contains metadata, page title, styles, and scripts.
<title>
Defines the page title shown in the browser tab.
<meta charset="UTF-8">
Specifies the character encoding of the document.
<meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0">
Ensures the page scales correctly on mobile devices.
<body>
Contains all the visible content of the page.
<h1>–<h6>
Heading tags; <h1> is the most important and <h6> is the least important.
<p>
Represents a paragraph of text.
<a href="...">
Defines a hyperlink to another page or resource.
<img src="..." alt="...">
Displays an image and requires the src and alt attributes.
<ul>
Creates an unordered (bulleted) list.
<ol>
Creates an ordered (numbered) list.
<li>
Defines an item inside a list.
<dl>, <dt>, <dd>
Defines a description list with terms and definitions.
<table>
Creates a table to display tabular data.
<tr>
Defines a row in a table.
<th>
Defines a table header cell.
<td>
Defines a table data cell.
<form>
Groups input controls for submitting data.
<input>
Creates a single-line input field for text, email, password, radio, checkbox, file, and more.
<label>
Labels a form control and improves accessibility.
<textarea>
Creates a multi-line text input area.
<select>
Creates a drop-down list.
<option>
Defines an option inside a select menu.
<optgroup>
Groups related options inside a select menu.
<button>
Represents a clickable button.
<div>
A block-level container used for grouping content.
<span>
An inline container used for styling small pieces of text.
<header>
Defines an introductory div for a page or div.
<nav>
Defines navigation links.
<div>
Defines a thematic div of content.
<article>
Defines self-contained content such as a blog post or news article.
<aside>
Defines content related to the main content, like a sidebar.
<footer>
Defines a footer for a div or page.

Image Tag and URL Types

The <img> tag embeds images into a page.

src
Specifies the image file URL.
alt
Provides alternative text if the image cannot load.
Absolute URL
A full path to an image, including protocol and domain, such as https://example.com/images/photo.jpg.
Relative URL
A path relative to the current page, such as images/photo.jpg or ../images/photo.jpg.
Note: This page contains the basic HTML tags and definitions for Day 1. Day 2 and Day 3 files may include additional examples and more advanced code.

CSS - Cascade Style Sheets

History of CSS

1994
CSS was first proposed by Håkon Wium Lie while working at CERN.
1996
CSS Level 1 (CSS1) was released with basic styling features.
1998
CSS Level 2 (CSS2) introduced positioning, z-index, and media types.
2011+
CSS3 moved to a modular format, adding transitions, animations, flexbox, and responsive design.
Today
CSS continues to grow with new modules and browser support for modern layout techniques.

Types of CSS

Inline CSS
Applied directly to an HTML element using the style attribute.
Example: <p style="color: red; font-size: 20px;">Text</p>
Inline CSS has the highest specificity and can override other styles.
Use it only for quick fixes or temporary testing, because it mixes content and presentation.
Internal CSS
Written inside a <style> block in the HTML <head>.
Example: <style> p { color: blue; } </style>
Internal CSS applies to the entire page and is useful for page-specific styling.
It is easier to manage than inline CSS but still stays inside the HTML file.
External CSS
Stored in a separate .css file and linked using the <link> tag.
Example: the current page uses ./day4_css.css.
External CSS is best for multi-page websites and cleaner HTML code.
It improves maintainability, reuse, and performance.
To increase rule importance: use !important, higher specificity, or IDs.

How HTML connects to CSS

The HTML file connects to an external CSS file using the <link> tag:

<link rel="stylesheet" href="./day4_css.css">

This line is placed inside the <head> section. It tells the browser to load the CSS file and apply its rules to the page.

External CSS is the best choice for larger websites because the same stylesheet can style multiple pages.

Examples of CSS Use

Inline CSS example:

This text uses inline CSS directly in the HTML tag.

Internal CSS example:

This text uses internal CSS inside the same HTML file.

External CSS example:

This text uses external CSS from day4_css.css.

Selectors

Selectors tell CSS which HTML elements should receive style rules.

Element Selector
Targets all elements of a given tag. Example: p { color: green; } affects every paragraph.
Class Selector
Targets elements with a specific class. Example: .highlight { font-weight: bold; }.
ID Selector
Targets a single element with a unique ID. Example: #main-title { font-size: 28px; }.
Group Selector
Targets multiple selectors at once. Example: h1, h2, p { margin: 0; }.
Pseudo-class Selector
Targets an element state like :hover, :focus, or :active.
Combinator Selector
Targets elements based on relationships, such as div p or ul > li.
child selector

Display Property

The display property defines how an element is rendered in the layout.

display: block;
Block elements take up the full width and start on a new line. Example: div, p.
display: inline;
Inline elements stay on the same line and only take as much width as needed. Example: span, a.
display: inline-block;
Inline-block elements act like inline elements but allow width and height to be set.
display: none;
Hides the element completely. It does not appear and does not occupy space.
display: flex;
Creates a flexible container to align and distribute space among items.
justify content

space
space around
apace between
space evenly
end
align-items

center
display: grid;
Creates a grid container with rows and columns for advanced layouts.
